title: SHE BROKE OPEN A FORTUNE AT THE FEET OF JESUS—AND WHAT HE SAID NEXT STILL EXPOSES THE HUMAN HEART
paragraphs: SHE BROKE OPEN A FORTUNE AT THE FEET OF JESUS—AND WHAT HE SAID NEXT STILL EXPOSES THE HUMAN HEART

Why did Mary of Bethany pour perfume worth nearly a year's wages on Jesus? The answer is more than a beautiful act of worship. It is a story of extravagant love, hidden betrayal, misunderstood devotion, and a Savior walking toward the cross. And somewhere between Mary's tears, Judas's objection, and the fragrance that filled the house, we may discover what our own hearts truly treasure.
There are moments in Scripture that are so quiet, so deeply human, that you can almost hear the breathing in the room.
A family gathered around a table.
The sound of people talking.
Food being served.
A man who had recently been dead, now sitting alive among the guests.
And a woman carrying something so expensive that breaking it open would cause everyone to notice.
Nobody in that room could have imagined how long her act would be remembered.
But Jesus knew.
He knew the cross was approaching.
He knew betrayal was already growing in a heart sitting near Him.
He knew the suffering waiting for Him in Jerusalem.
And while others were occupied with the dinner, Mary of Bethany approached Him with something she could never recover once it was poured out.
A costly perfume.
A possession worth almost a year's wages.
Perhaps one of the most valuable things she owned.
And then she did something that made people question her judgment.
She poured it on Jesus.
Not a drop.
Not a cautious little offering.
She anointed His feet and wiped them with her hair.
And John records one extraordinary detail.
“And the house was filled with the odour of the ointment.” — John 12:3, KJV
The whole house.
Think about that.
One woman's worship became impossible for everyone else to ignore.
But what makes this account so powerful is not simply the price of the perfume.
It is the fact that Jesus was about to die.
And Mary gave Him something precious while He was still there to receive it.
There is a question hidden in that moment that every believer eventually has to confront.
What is Jesus worth to you when loving Him costs you something?
Not when worship is convenient.
Not when obedience makes you look spiritual.
Not when following Him brings applause, comfort, or recognition.
But when surrender costs you something you genuinely treasure.
Because that evening in Bethany, one woman poured out what was precious.
And another disciple looked at the same act and saw only wasted money.
The difference between those two hearts should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Six days before the Passover, Jesus arrived in Bethany.
John 12:1 places the event near the final Passover before Christ's crucifixion. Jesus had already raised Lazarus from the dead, and the consequences of that miracle were still unfolding.
Imagine being Lazarus.
Imagine remembering the darkness of death, then hearing the voice of Jesus calling you out of the tomb.
Imagine sitting at dinner, eating ordinary food, surrounded by familiar faces, knowing that you were alive because the Son of God had spoken your name.
John tells us Lazarus was among those reclining at the table.
Martha was serving.
Mary was about to worship.
There is something beautiful about these details.
The family was together again.
The brother they had buried was alive.
The grief that had overwhelmed their home had been interrupted by the resurrection power of Christ.
But the miracle had not removed every shadow.
Jesus was moving toward His own death.
And the One who had called Lazarus out of the grave would soon enter a tomb Himself.
That is the breathtaking tension of this story.
A resurrected man was sitting at the table.
And the Resurrection and the Life was preparing to die.
Before we go further, we need to remember something about Mary.
This was not the first time Scripture placed her at the feet of Jesus.
In Luke 10:39, Mary sat at His feet and listened to His teaching while Martha was occupied with serving.
In John 11:32, Mary fell at His feet in grief after Lazarus died.
And now, in John 12:3, Mary is once again at His feet.
Listening.
Grieving.
Worshiping.
Three scenes.
Three profoundly different moments.
One consistent posture.
Mary knew where to bring her attention, her sorrow, and her devotion.
But we must be careful not to invent details Scripture never gives us.
The Bible does not identify Mary of Bethany as Mary Magdalene. Neither does it identify her as the unnamed sinful woman in Luke 7. Those women should not be automatically treated as the same person.
Mary of Bethany was the sister of Martha and Lazarus.
And the extraordinary thing about her is that John does not need to give us a dramatic history of scandal to show us the power of grace.
Her devotion is powerful precisely because she recognized something about Jesus that others were failing to appreciate.
She had listened to Him.
She had grieved before Him.
She had witnessed His power over death.
And now she would honor Him as He approached His burial.
John tells us:
“Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair.” — John 12:3, KJV
The original Greek adds richness to this scene.
John describes the perfume as:
μύρου νάρδου πιστικῆς πολυτίμου
myrou nardou pistikēs polytimou
This refers to costly perfume made from nard.
The word πολυτίμου (polytimou) means “very costly” or “of great value.”

The term πιστικῆς (pistikēs) has been interpreted in different ways, often understood as indicating genuine or pure nard. Its exact nuance is debated, so we should not build an entire spiritual doctrine on that one word.
What is unmistakable is the expense.
Judas later estimated its value at three hundred denarii.
A denarius was commonly associated with a day's wage for a laborer, as illustrated in Matthew 20:2.
Three hundred denarii, therefore, represented roughly the earnings of hundreds of working days.
This was no ordinary bottle of perfume.
It represented enormous economic value.
We do not know how Mary acquired it.
We do not know whether it was an inheritance, a gift, a family possession, or something purchased with years of savings.
Scripture does not tell us.
But we know it was precious.
And Mary chose to use it to honor Jesus.
Pause there.
Because we live in a world that teaches us to calculate the value of nearly everything.
How much does it cost?
What will I get in return?
Will people appreciate it?
Will this benefit me?
Will it be worth the sacrifice?
There is a place for wise stewardship. Scripture never praises carelessness merely because it is expensive.
But Mary was not trying to impress an audience.
She was honoring her Lord.
And that is what makes her act so searching.
She did not appear to be negotiating with Jesus.
She was not purchasing a miracle.
She was not buying forgiveness.
She was not giving in order to make God owe her something.
She was responding to the One who had already shown her family extraordinary mercy.
True worship is not a transaction through which we purchase God's love. It is a response to the love and grace we have received.
That distinction matters.
Because some people have spent their entire Christian lives believing that if they pray enough, give enough, serve enough, or sacrifice enough, perhaps God will finally accept them.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
We are not saved because our offerings are impressive.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
And the next verse reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace comes first.
A transformed life follows.
Mary's perfume did not purchase Christ's approval.
Her act expressed devotion to the Christ she loved.
And then came the moment that turned the dinner into a confrontation.
Judas Iscariot spoke.
“Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?” — John 12:5, KJV
At first, his objection sounded reasonable.
Three hundred denarii.
Think how many hungry people that money could help.
Think how much practical good it could accomplish.
Why pour something so valuable on someone's feet?
Why not use it for a cause everyone could recognize as worthwhile?
It sounded compassionate.
Responsible.
Even righteous.
But John exposes what was happening beneath the words.
“This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief.” — John 12:6, KJV
Judas kept the common moneybag and stole from what was placed in it.
His objection was not an honest disagreement over charitable priorities.
According to John's testimony, it was hypocrisy.
He used concern for the poor to conceal his own greed.
And here is where this account becomes painfully personal.
Because it is possible to speak the language of righteousness while hiding an entirely different motive.
It is possible to sound deeply spiritual while resisting the very Lord we claim to serve.
It is possible to criticize another person's devotion while neglecting our own obedience.
But this passage does not give us permission to accuse everyone who questions a ministry's spending of being like Judas.
Accountability is biblical.
Generosity toward the poor is biblical.
Financial integrity is biblical.
Jesus Himself affirmed the continuing presence and needs of the poor in John 12:8, echoing the concern of Deuteronomy 15:11.
The problem was not that Judas mentioned the poor.
The problem was that he did not genuinely care about them.
His words concealed a heart that wanted to take.
Mary's actions revealed a heart that wanted to honor Christ.
And the contrast could hardly be greater.
One disciple was calculating the price of the perfume.
One woman was expressing the worth of Jesus.
Judas saw what could have been placed in the moneybag.
Mary saw the Savior before her.
And before anyone could reduce her act to foolishness, Jesus spoke.
“Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this.” — John 12:7, KJV
These words deserve careful attention.
The Greek text includes the expression:
εἰς τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ ἐνταφιασμοῦ μου
eis tēn hēmeran tou entaphiasmou mou
It means “for the day of my burial.”
The word ἐνταφιασμοῦ (entaphiasmou) refers to burial or preparation for burial.
Jesus connected Mary's anointing to His approaching death.
There is a textual and translational difficulty in the full sentence of John 12:7, which is why English translations differ in how they express Mary's keeping of the perfume.
But the central point remains clear.
Jesus defended her action and gave it significance in relation to His burial.
We should not claim with certainty that Mary understood every detail of the crucifixion beforehand.
John does not explicitly tell us that.
What we can say is that Jesus interpreted her act in the light of His coming death.
And that changes everything.
Because this was not merely a sentimental moment at a dinner.
It was an act of devotion standing in the shadow of Calvary.
Soon Jesus would be arrested.
Soon He would be mocked.
Soon soldiers would strike Him.
Soon a crown of thorns would be pressed upon His head.
Soon nails would pierce His hands and feet.
Soon the One who raised Lazarus would willingly lay down His own life.
But before the brutality of the cross, there was this moment of tenderness.
Before hands would seize Him in violence, Mary's hands honored Him.
Before people would mock His kingship, Mary expressed reverence.
Before His body would be placed in a tomb, Jesus received an anointing He Himself connected with burial.
And suddenly, the perfume seems less like extravagance and more like love.
Not because money had ceased to matter.
But because the moment was extraordinary.
Jesus was approaching the once-for-all sacrifice through which sinners could be reconciled to God.
Mary's offering did not save the world.
Jesus would do that.
Her perfume could not wash away sin.
His blood would accomplish redemption.
Her devotion could not defeat death.
His resurrection would proclaim victory over it.
And this is where the story must lead us.
Not merely to admire Mary.
But to behold Christ.
Because if we finish this account thinking only about how much Mary gave, we have missed the infinitely greater gift.
Mary poured out costly perfume on Jesus. Jesus was preparing to give His life for sinners.
Her gift was extraordinary.
His grace is beyond calculation.
Her perfume filled a house.
The good news of His death and resurrection would be proclaimed to the nations.
And her act points us toward a Savior whose love cannot be measured in denarii, possessions, or earthly wealth.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying a burden no one else knows about.
Maybe your faith has become exhausted.
You still attend church.
You still know the songs.
You still say “God is good.”
But somewhere along the way, the fire of your first love began to fade.
You remember when prayer felt like communion instead of obligation.
You remember when opening Scripture felt like being welcomed into the presence of God.
You remember when the name of Jesus could move you to tears.
But now?
You are tired.
Distracted.
Wounded.
Perhaps disappointed by people who represented Christ poorly.
Perhaps ashamed of something you have never confessed.
Perhaps you have been hiding behind religious activity because facing your own heart feels unbearable.
And Mary's story brings a question that is both gentle and piercing.
When was the last time you came to Jesus simply because He is worthy?
Not to perform.
Not to prove something.
Not to earn a blessing.
But to surrender.
You may not have expensive perfume.
You may be struggling financially.
You may have nothing impressive to place before Him.
But the Lord does not measure your love by the size of your bank account.
Remember the poor widow in Mark 12:41–44.
Jesus noticed her small offering and understood its significance in light of what she had.
Remember the repentant tax collector in Luke 18:13–14.
He could barely lift his eyes toward heaven.
He simply pleaded for mercy.
And Jesus said he went home justified.
Remember the criminal beside Christ in Luke 23:42–43.
He had no opportunity to build a lifetime of religious accomplishments.
He turned to the crucified King in faith.
And Jesus promised him paradise.
Do you see it?
The Gospel is not reserved for people who can afford extravagant gifts.
It is for sinners who need a Savior.
For the broken.
For the ashamed.
For the proud who finally recognize their need to repent.
For those who have wandered far and those who have quietly grown cold while sitting in church.
For the person who thinks, “I have made too many mistakes for God to want me.”
Look at the cross.
Christ did not die because we were worthy enough to purchase His love.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became respectable.
Not after we learned to hide our failures behind religious language.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that death did not have the final word.
That is the hope of the Gospel.
Not that our past never happened.
Not that our sins were harmless.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
But that Jesus Christ can forgive, reconcile, and transform those who turn to Him in faith.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending evil was good.
He rewrites the future of those He redeems.
He takes the guilty who repent and brings them into forgiveness.
He calls the spiritually dead into new life.
He teaches the proud to become humble.
He brings the wandering home.
He restores people who believed their failures would always define them.
And He does it through His own death and resurrection, not through the price of anything we could offer.
There is another detail in Mary's story that I cannot stop thinking about.
The fragrance filled the house.
John could have recorded the anointing and moved on.
But he included the fragrance.
The aroma did not remain confined to Mary's hands.
It spread.
People who had not purchased the perfume could smell it.
People who had not understood her actions were still surrounded by its fragrance.
And while the text describes a literal event, it offers a beautiful picture of how sincere devotion to Christ can affect the people around us.
Your family may not remember every sermon you share.
Your children may not remember every religious phrase you use.
Your friends may forget the arguments you win.
But they may remember how you responded when you were wronged.
They may remember that you confessed when you sinned.
They may remember your patience when life became difficult.
They may remember that you cared for the overlooked.
They may remember that you refused to abandon your faith when following Jesus became costly.
They may remember the kindness you showed when nobody was watching.
And perhaps, through your life, they will catch a glimpse of the Savior you love.
Second Corinthians 2:14–15 speaks of believers spreading the knowledge of Christ and being a fragrance of Christ.
That does not mean every act of worship will attract universal approval.
Mary's certainly did not.
But faithfulness to Jesus can leave an impression far beyond the moment in which it occurs.
Sometimes we are so desperate to be noticed that we forget the purpose of Christian witness.
We are not called to make ourselves the center.
We are called to make Christ known.
Mary did not stand up and deliver a speech about her sacrifice.
She did not announce the price of the perfume.
She did not demand applause.
She simply honored Jesus.
And the Lord defended her.
There is freedom in that.
You do not have to turn every sacrifice into a performance.
You do not have to publish every good deed.
You do not have to convince everyone that your devotion is genuine.
You can serve quietly.
You can give responsibly.
You can forgive.
You can repent.
You can open your Bible when no one is looking.
You can care for someone who has nothing to offer you in return.
You can worship when your heart is heavy.
And you can trust that the Lord sees what people overlook.
But Mary's story also challenges us not to confuse emotion with obedience.
A moving worship service is not the same thing as a surrendered life.
Tears do not automatically equal repentance.
A generous donation does not erase unconfessed sin.
A Christian social media profile does not guarantee a heart that belongs to Christ.
Jesus said in John 14:15:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.” — KJV
Love for Jesus expresses itself in obedience.
Not perfect obedience that earns salvation.
But a real, growing response to His grace.
If we claim to love Him while deliberately protecting the sin He calls us to abandon, we need to examine our hearts.
If we celebrate Mary's sacrifice but refuse to forgive someone we have wronged, we need to listen again to Christ.
If we praise generosity while neglecting the vulnerable, we have misunderstood the God who commands justice and mercy.
If we speak constantly about Jesus but rarely listen to His Word, we need to return to His feet.
And if we have become more concerned with looking like Christians than actually following Christ, perhaps this is the moment to stop pretending.
Not because Jesus is unwilling to receive repentant sinners.
But because His grace is too precious to reduce to a religious appearance.
The same Savior who defended Mary calls us to come to Him in truth.
There is no need to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
There is no need to exaggerate your past.
There is no need to pretend you are healed from struggles that still require prayer, discipleship, wise counsel, and time.
Come honestly.
Come with your questions.
Come with your failures.
Come with your gratitude.
Come ready to turn from sin.
Come trusting not in the strength of your own devotion, but in the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
And maybe that is the deepest beauty of Mary's act.
She came to the feet of the One who would soon go to the cross.
She honored Him before the suffering.
She offered something precious without knowing how future generations would read her story.
And Jesus did not dismiss her.
He defended her.
The people in that room could debate the monetary value of her offering.
But Jesus understood its place in the unfolding story of His death.
And that should make us ask one more question.
What if the thing you need to surrender today is not money at all?
What if it is pride?
What if it is the bitterness you have carried for years?
What if it is the secret habit you keep promising to abandon?
What if it is your need to control everything?
What if it is the fear of being seen as weak?
What if it is your refusal to admit that you need help?
What if the most costly thing you can bring to Jesus today is an honest heart?
Not because surrender itself purchases salvation.
But because the grace of Christ calls us out of hiding and into the light.
First John 1:9 reminds us that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
And Psalm 51:17 speaks of the broken and contrite heart that God does not despise.
You do not need a room full of witnesses.
You do not need an expensive offering.
You need the Savior.
And if you have never placed your faith in Jesus Christ, the invitation of the Gospel is for you.
Repent and believe in Him.
He died for our sins and rose again, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Forgiveness and new life are found in Him.
Not in a donation.
Not in religious merchandise.
Not in public approval.
In Jesus Christ alone.
And if you already belong to Him, perhaps today is a call to renew your devotion.
To return to Scripture.
To return to prayer.
To love your neighbor.
To care for the poor.
To worship without pretending.
To follow Jesus not merely when it feels beautiful, but when obedience becomes costly.
Because the greatest question in John 12 is not whether Mary's perfume was expensive.
It is whether we recognize the worth of the One she anointed.
And if this story has exposed something in your own heart, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than leaving a casual reaction.
Be honest before God.
Or, if you feel comfortable, share what Jesus is teaching you about surrender.
You do not have to disclose private sins or painful details publicly. God hears the prayers you cannot put into words, too.
Because the Church is not supposed to be a gathering of people pretending to have no wounds.
We are people who need the same Savior.
We need His truth.
We need His grace.
We need one another.
And we need to keep returning to the Gospel.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to make a personality famous.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to turn devotion into merchandise.
But to help make Christ-centered teaching, Scripture, encouragement, and discipleship resources accessible to people who need them.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, deepen their prayer lives, recognize false teaching, strengthen their faith, and follow Jesus with greater maturity.
And I want to speak plainly about something important.
Producing, maintaining, and expanding resources like these requires time, effort, and practical support.
Not because you owe us something for receiving God's Word.
You do not.
And certainly not because a monthly payment can earn God's favor.
But because voluntary, faithful support can help this ministry continue creating resources, reaching more people, and keeping valuable Christian materials available without charge.

The New Testament teaches that those who benefit from spiritual instruction may share material support with those who teach (Galatians 6:6), and that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14).
It also teaches that giving should be willing, not pressured.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Those responsibilities matter.
Your family's essential needs matter.
Those products are simply an additional expression of appreciation, not the purpose of discipleship.
The greater purpose is to keep pointing people toward Christ.
Not merely to increase a number on a page.
Someone may have lost the joy of worship.
Someone may be carrying guilt.
Someone may be trying to earn a forgiveness Jesus freely offers.
Someone may have been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
Someone may be wondering whether God still receives people who have failed Him.
You cannot know exactly who will read what you share.
But you can offer them a truthful reminder of Christ.
Not every believer can give financially.
But every believer can seek to glorify God through faith, love, obedience, prayer, and faithful witness.
The mission is greater than any one platform.
The Savior is greater than any one ministry.
And His Gospel is too precious to be treated as a product that only paying supporters can receive.
Picture Lazarus at the table.
Martha serving.
Judas objecting.
Mary kneeling at the feet of Jesus.
The costly perfume poured out.
The fragrance moving through the room.
And Jesus, fully aware of the suffering ahead, receiving her act of devotion.
For a moment, forget the crowd.
Forget the argument.
Forget the money.
Look at Jesus.
The One who would carry the cross.
The One who would bear the judgment our sins deserved.
The One who would cry, “It is finished.”
The One who would rise from the grave.
The One who still calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through faith in His name.
Mary brought something precious to Him.
But Jesus would give something infinitely greater.
His life.
And that is where this story finds its true center.
Not in a bottle of perfume.
Not in the judgment of Judas.
Not even in the beauty of Mary's devotion.
But in the crucified and risen Christ.
The One worthy of worship before the cross.
The One who accomplished redemption at the cross.
The One who conquered death through His resurrection.
And the One worthy of our love, obedience, and praise today.
So when you finally close this article, I hope you remember more than the price of the perfume.
I hope you remember the Savior who defended Mary's devotion and then willingly walked toward Calvary.
I hope you remember that you cannot purchase His grace.
I hope you remember that repentance is not the end of hope, but the turning of a sinner toward the Savior who forgives.
And I hope you remember that even an ordinary life, surrendered to Christ, can bear witness to an extraordinary Redeemer.
Because one day, the perfume in that house would fade.
The dinner would end.
The guests would leave.
The fragrance would disappear.
But the Lord Mary worshiped would rise from the dead.
And the Gospel would continue to be proclaimed long after that evening in Bethany.
The fragrance faded from the house, but the love that carried Jesus to the cross will never lose its power to save.
